title: File:Yellow-tailed Black Cockatoos.ogg
name: Yellow-tailed Black Cockatoos
description: Audio recording of the eerie call of the Yellow-Tailed Black Cockatoo, a large cockatoo that inhabits much of south-eastern Australia, from the Eyre Peninsula in South Australia to south-east Queensland. Its call sometimes sounds similar to that portrayed in some sci-fi movies as emanating from the pterodactyl. However, in this recording, it mostly sounds like a horse's whinny! It was recorded at Thirlmere Lakes near Tahmoor, New South Wales, Australia.

title: File:2000 Body's 24 Hour Clock by Bill Nye for National Science Foundation.oga
name: 2000 Body's 24 Hour Clock by Bill Nye for National Science Foundation
description: "Body's 24 Hour Clock" -- Bill Nye for NSF50 How do our body clocks regulate our lives? Bill Nye lets us in on the secret. Credit: NSF Audio Transcript: (TICKING SOUND) "Don't be nervous. It's not a bomb. It's me, Bill Nye The Science Guy here to celebrate the National Science Foundation's 50th anniversary. The ticking you hear represents my body's 24-hour clock. You see we all have body clocks. In fact there's a cluster of cells In your brain that regulates stuff like your breathing, your heart rate, your digestion and your sleep/wake cycle. Your body clock also helps tell you when you're hungry, and scientists now believe that learning about our body clocks may help us lower blood pressure without drugs and even overcome jet lag. It's all part of new research funded by NSF focused on gaining control of our body clocks. I wonder if this means we can turn our clocks back? Hmmm. But for now, this is Bill Nye The Science Guy inviting you to join me and the National Science Foundation in celebrating fifty years of science and engineering discoveries."
author: National Science Foundation
